gap: No result ChatGPT got states how close a charger's on-screen watts are to a real meter: Notebookcheck put a Fnirsi FNB58 tester on the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W and saw 51 W on the charger's screen against about 49.5 W on the tester, so the readings can be 1–2 W off. None of them says either that the Baseus AH22 opens on a total-watts screen, so you tap through to another page to see each port.
standout_why: I read four of the cited rival pages: ChargerLAB's UGREEN 160W teardown, Macworld's Satechi ChargeView 240W review, the UGREEN Nexode Pro series page and techtest's AH22 review. ChargerLAB shows the UGREEN screen with C1 at 98 W and C2 at 55 W but never checks those numbers against its POWER-Z meter. Macworld lists per-port watts, total and cooling status, also with no meter check. UGREEN's own page only says 'Real-Time Charging Status'. ChatGPT's two answers say outright that it hadn't tested meter accuracy. Nobody explains that 'shows each port' can mean all ports on one screen (UGREEN in ChargerLAB's photo, Anker Prime 160W per Anker) or a second page you tap to (AH22 per Smartzone). Rivals already have part of this (that per-port screens exist), but the accuracy number and the tap-to-reach difference are new.
decides: This backs the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 5-Port (ours) as the pick for the 140 W tier. Its screen shows watts per port plus volts, amps (techtest) and protocol (Notebookcheck). It is the only display in the set that a named reviewer checked against a meter (within 1–2 W). Techtest also ran 140 W for 4 hours with no throttling. For the Baseus AH22 at 100 W, the page should say three things. First, the default screen is total watts and each port's watts are on a second page. Second, in Gentle mode the charger limits each port to about 20 W (techtest), so a low reading there is the limit working, not a fault. Third, it holds 100 W for about 40 minutes and then drops to 80 W (techtest). The Anker Prime 160W screen shows every port at once (Anker's wording), but its one-port rating is 150 W at 28 V/5.36 A, not the 140 W that PD 3.1 laptops use.
